overview: This file concerns postwar aviation policy in U.S.-occupied East Asia in 1948. An April telegram recommends against granting a French civil-air franchise in southern Korea because Gimpo’s facilities were inadequate and existing American carriers deserved priority. The remainder documents the State and War Departments’ response to Soviet questions in the Far Eastern Commission about the expensive reconstruction of Misawa Airfield: officials justified it as necessary for occupation aircraft, border-control operations, emergency landings, and eventual commercial aviation, while recommending that the United States not volunteer an explanation unless pressed.

subfiles.title: CINCFE telegram opposing a French civil-air franchise in Korea
subfiles.from: Commander in Chief, Far East (CINCFE), Tokyo
subfiles.to: Department of the Army; information to CG USAFIK, CG FEAF, and Department of State
subfiles.about: Recommends rejecting any French request for a civil-air franchise in Korea because Gimpo could not support more traffic.
subfiles.summary: The unsigned message reiterates that facilities at Kimpo Air Force Base were insufficient for additional air traffic and cites the unsettled economic conditions in southern Korea. If more civil-air franchises were authorized, it recommends giving priority first to Northwest Airlines and then to INAC. Because the French interest was considered indirect, any French application should be viewed unfavorably.

subfiles.title: Telegram to SCAP concerning Soviet questions about Misawa Airfield
subfiles.from: George C. Marshall, Department of State
subfiles.to: Acting Political Adviser, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, Tokyo; information to Army Chief of Staff
subfiles.about: Alerts SCAP that Soviet questions about the purpose, cost, and post-treaty fate of Misawa Airfield might be raised again.
subfiles.summary: A Soviet member of the Far Eastern Commission’s Steering Committee cited Lindsay Parrott’s May 3 New York Times article, which described a $13 million field capable of handling heavy bombers and jet aircraft. He asked why such construction was necessary near the end of the occupation, what would happen to the field after a peace treaty, and whether it might be destroyed. The Department of State was consulting the Air Force about whether and how the United States should answer.

subfiles.title: War Department explanation of the improvement of Misawa Airfield
subfiles.from: Major General Daniel Noce, Chief, Civil Affairs Division
subfiles.to: P. P. Claxton, Department of State
subfiles.about: Explains the military and civil-aviation reasons for reconstructing Misawa and other Japanese airfields.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum says occupation surveys found Japanese runways too short and weak for high-performance American aircraft. SCAP consequently authorized improvements to a chain of fields, including Misawa on May 1, 1946, for occupation contingencies, anti-smuggling and illegal-entry patrols, and emergency landings. Material and personnel shortages delayed the work, but the completed improvements increased flight safety. The facilities were expected to revert to Japan after the occupation unless prohibited by the peace treaty and might support authorized commercial aviation.

subfiles.title: Claxton cover memorandum on the Misawa inquiry
subfiles.about: Reports Claxton’s discussion with General Noce and forwards a copy of the memorandum requesting information about Misawa.
subfiles.summary: Claxton states that he discussed the Misawa matter with General Noce. Noce asked for a written memorandum, which Claxton sent and attached in copy for Saltzman’s information.

subfiles.title: Claxton memorandum requesting an investigation of Misawa Airfield
subfiles.from: P. P. Claxton Jr., Department of State
subfiles.to: Major General Daniel Noce, Chief, Civil Affairs Division, Department of the Army
subfiles.about: Requests exact information with which to answer anticipated Far Eastern Commission criticism of Misawa and similar airfields.
subfiles.summary: Claxton recounts the Soviet member’s questions about Lindsay Parrott’s article and notes that an Air Force spokesman in Tokyo had confirmed the field’s existence. He suggests that Misawa could be defended internationally only as an occupation necessity, while observing that Japan’s peaceful conditions made a military-uprising rationale difficult unless construction began early. He asks for a thorough investigation of the field’s characteristics, authority, purposes, and construction circumstances, as well as information on comparable airports.

subfiles.title: Draft guidance to the U.S. member of the Far Eastern Commission
subfiles.to: United States Member, Far Eastern Commission
subfiles.about: Advises the U.S. member not to volunteer an answer about Misawa but authorizes use of an attached statement if the issue is raised again.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum reviews the Soviet member’s references to the New York Times article at the May 4 Steering Committee meeting and during the May 6 discussion of civil aviation in Japan. Because the U.S. member had never agreed to supply information, Saltzman recommends against volunteering a response. If Soviet or other members renew the inquiry, however, the U.S. member may communicate the substance of the enclosed statement.

subfiles.title: Proposed statement defending Misawa Airfield improvements
subfiles.from: United States Member, Far Eastern Commission, as drafted by the Department of State
subfiles.to: Members of the Far Eastern Commission
subfiles.about: Provides a prepared explanation that Misawa was improved to make the occupation effective and aviation safer.
subfiles.summary: The proposed statement says Japan’s existing airfields could not safely handle American high-performance aircraft, prompting SCAP to improve a chain of fields for occupation contingencies, anti-smuggling operations, prevention of illegal entry, and emergency landings. Shortages delayed authorization for Misawa until May 1, 1946, after which its runways were strengthened and extended and servicing facilities added. These improvements were said to permit military and authorized commercial aircraft to operate with greater safety.

interest: The file shows how an engineering project became a diplomatic problem as Soviet representatives questioned whether a major airfield was compatible with an occupation supposedly nearing its end. Its sequence of inquiry, interdepartmental explanation, and carefully qualified talking points reveals how U.S. officials developed—and controlled—the public rationale for Misawa. The Korean telegram also usefully connects limited airfield capacity to competition over early postwar commercial routes and franchises.
